disposition_reason: FDA perspective/review on Cd and Pb in cocoa and chocolate. Mostly context, but Table 1 prints the only numeric origin-stratified (Africa vs Latin America) means for the Abt 2018 US retail dataset and previously unpublished FDA results for Asian-origin products (Abt et al. 2019 ACS meeting), plus EU and Codex Cd MLs and a narrative review of farm, post-harvest and blending mitigation.
disposition_locator: Table 1 (pp. C-D); Table 2 (p. D); Table 3 and Codex ML text (p. E); Mitigation Efforts and Discussion (pp. E-F)

study.design: review (perspective) with summary table of selected occurrence studies
study.material_scope: cocoa powder, cocoa nibs, dark and milk chocolate, chocolate unspecified (as summarised from cited studies)
study.growing_origin_vs_market: Table 1 is organised by bean growing origin (continent; region/country where reported). For Dahiya, Devi and Jalbani the location is the purchase location (footnote c). Abt et al. rows are US-purchased products with label-declared origin.

controls.control: Raise soil pH with liming material
controls.outcome: Cited (Ramtahal 2018/2019, refs 32, 37, 38): liming decreases Cd phytoavailability and cacao Cd, but can also reduce Zn availability; no numbers given here.
Ramtahal et al. 2019 (ref 37): effective at reducing leaf Cd in vitro and in greenhouse, effectiveness reduced under field conditions (landscape, soil, rainfall, root depth); no numbers given here.
Higher soil Zn decreases Cd absorption (Kirkham 2006, ref 38); no numbers.
Decrease in soil chloride decreases Cd absorption, inferred from other crops (ref 39); no numbers.
Reduces Cd mobility by adsorption/complexation (ref 40); no numbers.
Zug et al. 2019 (Peru farms, ref 36): reduced fertilizer use may mitigate cacao Cd; no numbers given here.

controls.control: Agroforestry / shade trees (e.g. banana) instead of monoculture
controls.outcome: Gramlich et al. 2017 (Bolivia, ref 35): lower leaf Cd in agroforestry systems; Zug et al. surmise phytoremediation by shade trees; no numbers given here.

controls.comparator: 10 cacao accessions grown on soil of the same Cd concentration (Trinidad)
controls.outcome: Lewis et al. (ref 54): 13-fold variation in bean Cd and 7-fold variation in leaf Cd among 10 accessions.

controls.control: Extended fermentation lowering nib pH below 5
controls.outcome: Vanderschueren et al. (ref 55): Cd migrated from nib to seed coat when nib pH dropped below 5 after extended fermentation; flavour trade-off; no numbers given here.
Can significantly reduce Cd in cocoa and chocolate (ref 1); not possible for fine-flavour single-region chocolate; no numbers.

controls.control: Mitigation hierarchy (Meter et al. 2019): avoid high-risk areas for new plantations; manage Cd sources and amend soils; post-harvest steps (fermenting, drying, roasting, winnowing); blending
controls.outcome: Framework only; authors note considerable research needed on post-harvest step effectiveness.

controls.control: Pb good agricultural and manufacturing practice (Codex CAC/RCP 56-2004): avoid leaded gasoline, select low-Pb ingredients, avoid Pb solder in processing and storage equipment
controls.outcome: No measured effect. Review identifies post-harvest Pb entry points: soil/dust and emissions during fermentation and drying, Pb-contaminated shell fragments during shelling/winnowing, Pb soldering in small-scale equipment and storage containers.

controls.control: Partitioning of metals at pressing (formulation relevance of non-fat cocoa solids)
controls.comparator: cocoa butter vs non-fat cocoa solids
controls.outcome: Cd partitions mainly into non-fat cocoa solids; 10-15% of Pb partitions into cocoa butter (Mounicou 2003, ref 14).

contradictions_with_stored_summary: Stored summary says JECFA estimated cocoa Cd at 30-69% of total Cd intake in children 0.5-12 y and noted a cumulative concern; primary says total dietary Cd for high cocoa consumers was 30-69% of the PTMI for adults and 96% for children 0.5-12 y, and JECFA did not consider it of concern.
Stored summary lists Brazil among higher-Cd Latin American origins; primary says Latin America has higher Cd "with the exception of Brazil" and that several studies found lower Cd in Brazilian cocoa.

Stored summary says Pb "tracks anthropogenic deposition"; primary emphasises that cited studies attribute Pb in chocolate mainly to the production process and post-harvest contamination, with Pb not following origin patterns.

Stored summary cites Codex work "through CCCF14-17"; primary cites CCCF13 (2019) and states Codex MLs of 0.8 mg/kg (>=50 to <70% total cocoa solids, dry matter) and 0.9 mg/kg (>=70%), which the summary omits.
Stored summary omits Table 1 entirely, including the origin-stratified Abt 2018 means and the Abt et al. 2019 Asian-origin data, and omits the EU ML values (0.10/0.30/0.80/0.60 mg/kg).

Stored summary lists processing equipment and packaging as Pb sources; primary lists fermentation/drying exposure to soil, dust and emissions, shell fragments at winnowing, and Pb solder in equipment and storage containers (packaging not mentioned).
unresolved: Abt et al. 2019 ACS-meeting Asia data (ref 22): purchase market, collection dates, analytical method, LOD and basis are not given; values are taken as printed. Asia nib row n=1 printed without SD and recorded as sample_value statistic.

Secondary-citation rows (Bertoldi, Dahiya, Devi, Iwegbue, Jalbani, Lee and Low, Mounicou, Vanderschueren, Villa) are transcribed from Table 1 for completeness; units are ug/kg as the table header states, but the basis and censoring of each cited study are not given here and should come from the primary studies. Several (Dahiya, Devi, Jalbani, Iwegbue) concern chocolate candies of uncertain cocoa content.

Table 1 layout: header says Africa / Asia / Latin America columns; Lee and Low (Malaysia) and Mounicou Malaysia rows sit in the Asia column; Dahiya/Devi/Jalbani rows sit in the Asia column but are purchase locations (footnote c).
EU Table 3 first category is printed as "≤30% total dry cocoa solids"; the wording of Regulation 488/2014 itself (milk chocolate with <30%) was not checked here.
Collection period not applicable to the review; for Abt 2018 rows the period is Dec 2015-Jan 2016 per that paper.
notes: Exposure context: FDA TDS 2014-16 estimate (Spungen 2019, ref 12): all sweets including chocolate contribute 1.2% of children's dietary Cd and 3.5% of dietary Pb; JECFA 2013: high consumers of cocoa products 30-69% of PTMI (adults) and 96% (children 0.5-12 y). Cross-check: Abt 2018 origin-group means here reconcile with that paper's form means when weighted with its unclassified-origin caption means (e.g. dark chocolate Cd (8x105.4 + 26x424.7 + 23x160)/57 = 273 ug/kg vs Table 3 0.27 mg/kg; cocoa powder Pb (6x61.9 + 13x170.1 + 20x90)/39 = 112 vs 0.11 mg/kg).
